title: Mental Health — Antipsychotics: Classes, Administration & Teaching (Set 10)
subtitle: Typical vs atypical, indications, long-acting injectables, time course, adherence, client teaching & monitoring (side-effect recognition is covered in Set 6)
scenario: Understanding antipsychotic medications at a psychiatric-technician level—what they treat, the difference between typical and atypical agents, long-acting injectables, expected time course, supporting adherence, and teaching clients and families—while monitoring for and reporting side effects.

steps.q: Antipsychotic medications are used primarily to treat:

opts.text: Psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking, as seen in schizophrenia
opts.rat: Antipsychotics target psychotic symptoms—hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking—and are a mainstay of treatment for schizophrenia and other psychotic conditions.

opts.text: Simple tiredness with no other symptoms
opts.rat: Ordinary tiredness is not an indication for antipsychotic medication.

opts.text: A minor skin rash
opts.rat: A skin rash is not treated with antipsychotics.

opts.text: Seasonal allergies
opts.rat: Allergies are unrelated to antipsychotic therapy.

steps.q: First-generation ('typical') antipsychotics, such as haloperidol, are especially associated with:

opts.text: No side effects at all
opts.rat: All antipsychotics can cause side effects; typicals are notable for movement effects.

opts.text: Extrapyramidal (movement) side effects
opts.rat: First-generation antipsychotics are particularly associated with extrapyramidal symptoms—movement-related side effects such as dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. (Confirm drug examples with faculty; specific side-effect recognition is taught in Set 6.)

opts.text: Improved appetite as the main effect
opts.rat: Appetite change is not the defining feature of typical antipsychotics; movement effects are.

opts.text: Curing the illness permanently in one dose
opts.rat: Antipsychotics manage symptoms over time; they do not cure the illness in a single dose.

steps.q: Second-generation ('atypical') antipsychotics, such as olanzapine and risperidone, are associated more than typicals with:

opts.text: Having no monitoring needs
opts.rat: Atypicals require monitoring, particularly for metabolic effects.

opts.text: Causing severe movement effects far more often than typicals
opts.rat: Atypicals generally cause fewer movement (extrapyramidal) effects than typicals, though they still can occur.

opts.text: Metabolic effects such as weight gain and elevated blood glucose and lipids
opts.rat: Atypical antipsychotics are more associated with metabolic effects—weight gain and elevated blood glucose and lipids—so metabolic monitoring is important. (Confirm drug examples with faculty.)

opts.text: Being completely free of side effects
opts.rat: No antipsychotic is free of side effects.

steps.q: An important teaching point about how quickly antipsychotics work is that:

opts.text: They cure all symptoms within a few hours
opts.rat: Full antipsychotic effect is not immediate; it develops over time.

opts.text: They only work if taken once and then stopped
opts.rat: Ongoing, consistent use is needed; stopping early undermines treatment.

opts.text: They never help psychotic symptoms
opts.rat: Antipsychotics do reduce psychotic symptoms over time.

opts.text: Full effect may take days to weeks, so the client should keep taking it even before feeling a big change
opts.rat: While agitation may ease sooner, the full antipsychotic effect on hallucinations and delusions can take days to weeks. Clients should be encouraged to continue the medication consistently. (Confirm expected time frames with faculty.)

steps.q: For a client who often forgets daily oral doses and then relapses, the prescriber may order:

opts.text: A long-acting injectable (depot) antipsychotic given by injection at spaced intervals
opts.rat: Long-acting injectable (depot) antipsychotics are given by injection at spaced intervals (rather than daily pills), which can help clients who struggle with daily adherence. (Confirm specific dosing intervals with faculty.)

opts.text: Stopping medication altogether
opts.rat: Stopping medication would increase, not reduce, the risk of relapse.

opts.text: Doubling every missed oral dose without guidance
opts.rat: Doubling doses is unsafe; dose changes require prescriber direction.

opts.text: Switching to an over-the-counter vitamin
opts.rat: A vitamin does not treat psychosis or replace an antipsychotic.

steps.q: The main advantage of a long-acting injectable antipsychotic is that it:

opts.text: Works instantly with no time needed
opts.rat: Injectable form does not eliminate the general time course of antipsychotic effect.

opts.text: Supports adherence by removing the need for daily pills, helping prevent relapse
opts.rat: Because it is given at spaced intervals instead of daily, a long-acting injectable can improve adherence and help prevent relapse in clients who have trouble taking pills every day.

opts.text: Has no side effects because it is an injection
opts.rat: The route does not remove side effects; the same drug effects apply.

opts.text: Means the client never needs follow-up
opts.rat: Clients on injectables still need follow-up, monitoring, and support.

steps.q: Besides schizophrenia, antipsychotic medications may also be used to help with:

opts.text: Preventing the common cold
opts.rat: Antipsychotics have no role in preventing colds.

opts.text: Lowering cholesterol
opts.rat: Antipsychotics are not cholesterol-lowering drugs; some actually raise lipids.

opts.text: Acute agitation and the manic phase of bipolar disorder
opts.rat: Antipsychotics are also used to manage acute agitation and are commonly used in the manic phase of bipolar disorder, among other uses. (Confirm specific indications with faculty.)

opts.text: Healing a broken bone
opts.rat: Antipsychotics have no role in bone healing.

steps.q: For a client on an atypical antipsychotic, helpful teaching to reduce metabolic risk includes:

opts.text: Avoiding all physical activity
opts.rat: Inactivity worsens metabolic risk; regular activity helps.

opts.text: Skipping all health checkups
opts.rat: Regular monitoring of weight, glucose, and lipids is important, not skipping checkups.

opts.text: Eating high-sugar foods freely
opts.rat: A high-sugar diet increases metabolic risk and is not advised.

opts.text: A balanced diet, regular physical activity, and keeping scheduled weight, glucose, and lipid checks
opts.rat: Supporting a healthy diet, regular activity, and keeping scheduled metabolic monitoring (weight, blood glucose, lipids) helps manage the metabolic effects associated with atypical antipsychotics.

steps.q: Clozapine has a distinct place among antipsychotics because it is:

opts.text: Generally reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and requires regular blood monitoring
opts.rat: Clozapine can help clients who have not responded to other antipsychotics (treatment-resistant schizophrenia), but it requires regular blood monitoring for a serious drop in white cells. (Specific blood-count monitoring is detailed in Set 6; confirm protocol with faculty.)

opts.text: The first drug tried for every new client, with no monitoring
opts.rat: Clozapine is not first-line and requires close blood monitoring.

opts.text: An over-the-counter sleep aid
opts.rat: Clozapine is a prescription antipsychotic with special monitoring, not an OTC sleep aid.

opts.text: Free of any serious risks
opts.rat: Clozapine carries serious risks, which is why blood monitoring is required.

steps.q: A client starting an antipsychotic reports feeling dizzy and lightheaded when standing up quickly. Appropriate teaching is to:

opts.text: Stand up as fast as possible to get past the feeling
opts.rat: Rising quickly worsens orthostatic dizziness and increases fall risk.

opts.text: Change positions slowly—sit up, pause, then stand—because of orthostatic (postural) hypotension
opts.rat: Some antipsychotics cause orthostatic hypotension (a drop in blood pressure on standing). Teaching the client to change positions slowly helps prevent dizziness and falls.

opts.text: Stop drinking fluids
opts.rat: Reducing fluids can worsen low blood pressure and dizziness.

opts.text: Ignore it, as it is never related to the medication
opts.rat: Dizziness on standing can be a medication effect and should be addressed, not ignored.

steps.q: Because some antipsychotics can cause increased sensitivity to sunlight (photosensitivity), the technician should teach the client to:

opts.text: Spend extra time in direct midday sun to build tolerance
opts.rat: Extra sun exposure increases the risk of burns with photosensitivity.

opts.text: Stop the medication whenever it is sunny
opts.rat: The client should not stop the medication; they should protect their skin.

opts.text: Use sunscreen and protective clothing and limit direct sun exposure
opts.rat: For photosensitivity, teach the client to protect their skin—use sunscreen, wear protective clothing, and limit direct sun exposure—to prevent sunburn.

opts.text: Apply heat to the skin after sun exposure
opts.rat: Applying heat does not address photosensitivity and could worsen skin irritation.

steps.q: A client worries that antipsychotic medication is 'addictive.' The accurate teaching is that antipsychotics:

opts.text: Are addictive controlled substances like opioids
opts.rat: Antipsychotics are not addictive controlled substances.

opts.text: Cause a 'high' that clients crave
opts.rat: Antipsychotics do not produce a euphoric high or craving.

opts.text: Should be shared with others who have similar symptoms
opts.rat: Medications are individually prescribed and must never be shared.

opts.text: Are not addictive; however, they should not be stopped abruptly without the prescriber
opts.rat: Antipsychotics are not addictive and do not cause a craving 'high.' Even so, they should not be stopped abruptly on the client's own—changes should be made with the prescriber.

steps.q: When antipsychotics are considered for an older adult with dementia, an important safety point is that:

opts.text: They carry a boxed warning of increased risk of death in older adults with dementia and should be used cautiously and only when clearly needed
opts.rat: Antipsychotics carry a boxed warning about an increased risk of death when used for behavioral symptoms in older adults with dementia; they are used cautiously, only when clearly needed, and are closely monitored. (Confirm the current warning with faculty.)

opts.text: They are completely risk-free in older adults
opts.rat: They are not risk-free; there is a specific safety warning for older adults with dementia.

opts.text: They should be used routinely for any restlessness
opts.rat: Routine use for restlessness is not appropriate; nonpharmacologic approaches are tried first and use is cautious.

opts.text: They improve memory and reverse dementia
opts.rat: Antipsychotics do not treat or reverse dementia.

steps.q: When a client on a typical antipsychotic develops movement (extrapyramidal) side effects, the prescriber may order:

opts.text: A higher dose of the same antipsychotic to push through it
opts.rat: Increasing the antipsychotic would typically worsen movement side effects, not relieve them.

opts.text: An anticholinergic medication (such as benztropine) to help relieve the extrapyramidal symptoms
opts.rat: Anticholinergic medications such as benztropine are commonly ordered to relieve certain extrapyramidal (movement) side effects of antipsychotics. (Confirm specific medications and use with faculty.)

opts.text: A stimulant to increase the movements
opts.rat: A stimulant would not treat extrapyramidal symptoms and could worsen agitation.

opts.text: No action, since movement effects are always permanent
opts.rat: Many acute movement effects are treatable; they are not simply left untreated.

steps.q: Regarding stopping an antipsychotic, the technician should teach that:

opts.text: The client can quit anytime with no consequences
opts.rat: Abrupt or unsupervised stopping can lead to withdrawal effects or relapse.

opts.text: Doubling the dose is the way to stop
opts.rat: Doubling the dose is unsafe and is not how a medication is discontinued.

opts.text: It should not be stopped abruptly on one's own; any changes should be made with the prescriber to avoid withdrawal or relapse
opts.rat: Antipsychotics should not be stopped abruptly without guidance; abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal effects or symptom relapse, so changes are made with the prescriber.

opts.text: Stopping is required as soon as symptoms improve
opts.rat: Improvement is a sign the medication is working; continuing as prescribed helps prevent relapse.

steps.q: Because some antipsychotics cause sedation (drowsiness), the technician should:

opts.text: Encourage the client to drive right after the first dose to test themselves
opts.rat: Driving while sedated is dangerous; the client should know how the medication affects them first.

opts.text: Tell the client sedation means the drug is not working
opts.rat: Sedation is a side effect, not a sign the medication is ineffective.

opts.text: Ignore drowsiness entirely
opts.rat: Drowsiness affects safety and should be monitored and addressed.

opts.text: Monitor for drowsiness and caution the client about driving or operating machinery until they know how the medication affects them
opts.rat: Sedation can impair alertness. The technician should monitor for drowsiness and advise caution with driving or machinery until the client knows how the medication affects them.

steps.q: Compared with typical antipsychotics, atypical antipsychotics may offer more benefit for:

opts.text: Negative symptoms such as social withdrawal and flat affect, in addition to positive symptoms
opts.rat: Atypical antipsychotics may help negative symptoms (like withdrawal and flat affect) as well as positive symptoms, whereas typicals mainly target positive symptoms. (Confirm specifics with faculty.)

opts.text: Curing the illness so no further treatment is needed
opts.rat: No antipsychotic cures schizophrenia; ongoing treatment is generally needed.

opts.text: Eliminating the need for any monitoring
opts.rat: Atypicals require monitoring, especially metabolic monitoring.

opts.text: Treating symptoms only if taken once
opts.rat: Consistent ongoing use is needed for benefit.

steps.q: For a client who becomes acutely agitated and is at risk of harming self or others, a PRN (as-needed) antipsychotic may be used to:

opts.text: Punish the client for the behavior
opts.rat: Medication is never used as punishment; that would be chemical restraint.

opts.text: Help calm the client and reduce the risk of harm, together with verbal de-escalation and a safe environment
opts.rat: A PRN antipsychotic may be used to help calm acute agitation and reduce the risk of harm, alongside verbal de-escalation and environmental measures—not as a substitute for them or as punishment.

opts.text: Replace the need for any staff interaction
opts.rat: Medication supports, but does not replace, therapeutic interaction and de-escalation.

opts.text: Sedate the client purely for staff convenience
opts.rat: Medicating for staff convenience rather than the client's need is chemical restraint and is not acceptable.

steps.q: During antipsychotic therapy, the psychiatric technician's role includes:

opts.text: Adjusting the client's dose independently
opts.rat: Dose adjustments are made by the prescriber, not independently by the technician.

opts.text: Discouraging the client from taking prescribed medication
opts.rat: The technician supports adherence to prescribed medication, not discourages it.

opts.text: Observing for side effects, encouraging adherence, ensuring the dose is taken, and reporting concerns to the nurse
opts.rat: The technician observes for therapeutic and side effects, supports adherence, ensures the medication is actually taken, documents, and reports concerns to the supervising nurse.

opts.text: Ignoring reported side effects to avoid extra work
opts.rat: Side effects must be monitored and reported, never ignored.

steps.q: Overall, the goal of antipsychotic therapy is to:

opts.text: Keep the client as sedated as possible at all times
opts.rat: Over-sedation is not the goal; symptom control with the best possible functioning is.

opts.text: Stop the medication as soon as any effect appears
opts.rat: Stopping early risks relapse; therapy is continued as prescribed.

opts.text: Use the highest possible dose regardless of side effects
opts.rat: The aim is the lowest effective dose with side effects managed, not the highest dose.

opts.text: Reduce psychotic symptoms and support the client's functioning, while monitoring for and managing side effects
opts.rat: The goal is to reduce psychotic symptoms and help the client function as fully as possible, using an effective dose while monitoring for and managing side effects.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Mental Health Care (psychopharmacology — antipsychotics). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references at an introductory level. Drug names and classifications (haloperidol as typical; olanzapine/risperidone as atypical; clozapine for treatment-resistant; benztropine as an anticholinergic for EPS), long-acting-injectable dosing intervals, indications beyond schizophrenia, the boxed warning in older adults with dementia, and expected time frames are marked for faculty confirmation. No specific doses or lab values are asserted; detailed side-effect recognition (EPS/NMS/agranulocytosis) is covered in Set 6 (mh-core-06). Pending faculty review.
